extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and university mathematics instructors interested in proof teaching, assessment, and comprehension
extracted.subtask_description: Literature-review guidance on evaluating, teaching, and researching undergraduate mathematical proofs: what makes proofs good, how mathematicians grade proofs, and instructional tools/strategies to support students' proof comprehension and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a well-written proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “the most important characteristics of a well-written proof are logical correctness, clarity, fluency, and demonstration of understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professors in the cited study agreed on these four characteristics; however, they gave fluency issues (notation, layout, grammar, punctuation) little weight in the overall score. Use these four dimensions as primary evaluative axes when judging student proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring influenced by teachers' models of student understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians assigned points based not primarily on the correctness of the written artifact, but rather based on their models of students’ understanding; they sometimes did not assign full credit to proofs they evaluated as correct (primarily due to minor omissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variability and idiosyncrasy in scoring: deductions may reflect inferred student knowledge rather than the explicit written proof; small omissions can lead to point loss even if the argument is essentially correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts' reading: attend to logical structure and implicit warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Compared with undergraduates, mathematicians shift attention between consecutive lines, devote more effort to inferring implicit warrants, and attend more to logical structure rather than surface features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should encourage reading strategies that alternate between lines and integrate information to infer warrants; assessments of comprehension should probe ability to infer implicit logical links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novices' reading: focus on surface features
rubrics_metrics.description: Undergraduate students spend proportionately more time focusing on 'surface features' of arguments, suggesting they attend less to logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should explicitly redirect attention from surface/formal features to deeper logical structure (e.g., via training, scaffolds, or self-explanation prompts).

rubrics_metrics.name: High-quality proof summaries reference logical structure and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: In a study asking for 40-word summaries, high-scoring summaries referenced a proof's logical structure and 'the mechanism by which it reached a contradiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching summarization of proofs, train students to identify and concisely state the proof's top-level logical skeleton and key inference mechanism (e.g., how contradiction is reached).

rubrics_metrics.name: DNR instructional principles for teaching induction
rubrics_metrics.description: DNR system = Duality, Necessity, Repeated Reasoning. Duality distinguishes ways of thinking and ways of understanding; Necessity: students learn if they see an intellectual need; Repeated Reasoning: students must practice reasoning to internalize ways of thinking and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DNR to design induction instruction: make the intellectual need explicit, provide repeated reasoning opportunities, and address both procedural thinking and conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual proofs vs formal induction — students' procedural linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Students familiar with formal induction often link their knowledge intimately to algebraic, procedural methods and have difficulty using visual proofs to justify theorems; novices may use visuals only as inductive generalizations and not see them as establishing necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume visual proofs automatically confer explanatory understanding; instruction should make explicit how visual arguments establish necessity and connect to formal proof methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic-example selection principles (Rowland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for selecting generic examples: (1) The particular case should be neither too trivial nor too complicated. (2) In number theory, pick a number (e.g., 17) that one can easily follow through in a generic proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using generic examples in proofs, choose cases that are representative but tractable; stress/ignore key features to highlight the general role of the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing and using examples in proof activity (Ellis et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons for example choice: (1) test boundaries of a hypothesis, (2) examine relevant properties to the conjecture, (3) build a progression of specific examples. Uses of examples: (1) attend to common features across examples, (2) identify structure of a general argument, (3) envision an example as a changing representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students explicit strategies for selecting examples (boundary cases, property-focused, progressive sequences) and for using them to abstract common structure and structure-generalization of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and linguistic conventions of proof writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The linguistic conventions of mathematical proof are part of the genre; students often are unaware of these conventions or that they apply to proof writing (e.g., how mathematicians introduce objects; certain phrasings like 'None of the sets are ∅' may be objectionable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should include explicit teaching of genre conventions: how to introduce objects, standard phrasing, and acceptable/dispreferred linguistic choices in formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values and norms for written proofs (Dawkins & Weber)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of norms: (1) Justification in a proof should be deductive and not admit rebuttals. (2) Mathematical knowledge and justification should be independent of nonmathematical contexts, including time and author. (3) Proof is an autonomous object and not a description of the actual problem solving involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these norms to frame expectations for rigor and generality in written proofs; clarify to students how deductive justification and autonomy of proof relate to acceptable proof-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof frameworks: top-level logical structure representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof framework is a representation of the 'top-level' logical structure of a proof, rich enough to allow reconstruction of the statement being proved; a written representation might be a sequence of statements with blank spaces to be expanded into a full proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide students with proof frameworks/templates as scaffolds to build proofs; further research needed on effectiveness, but frameworks can help students focus on top-level reasoning before filling in details.

rubrics_metrics.name: e-Proofs: design intent and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: e-Proofs (e.g., 'graying out' less relevant parts to make structure explicit) were intended to reveal proof structure, but in testing students who studied an e-Proof did not learn more and retained knowledge less well—e-Proofs 'made learning feel easier' causing shallower engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use e-Proof resources cautiously: they may be less effective for first-time learners; consider using them for students who have already independently studied a proof and need clarification on specific confusing aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-explanation training for proof comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials instructed students to identify key ideas in each line of a proof and to explain each line in terms of other ideas in the proof and their own knowledge; students receiving this training were better at inferring warrants, relating different lines of a proof, and were more goal driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate self-explanation prompts/activities into instruction: line-by-line explanation tasks can improve students' ability to infer logical warrants and connect proof components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students' difficulty translating informal arguments into formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may 'see' why a proposition is true but lack means to express it as an explicit argument; they attend to only a small cross section of what can be carried forward from an informal argument toward creating a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should explicitly scaffold the transformation from informal reasoning to formal proofs, helping students identify which informal elements can be formalized and how to carry them forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback interpretation and revision behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When professors wrote comments on proofs, participants could usually identify the changes; when comments were clarification requests without providing new text, participants struggled to provide a rationale; when revising, participants mostly implemented suggested changes even without fully understanding the rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design feedback to include concrete suggestions or model text where possible; consider requiring revision and resubmission (with credit) to help students improve despite partial understanding of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians' judgments of explanatory value are consistent but sometimes disagree with literature claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Using comparative judgement, mathematicians showed extremely high agreement assessing explanatory value of proofs, but their assessments sometimes contradicted claims about which proof types are explanatory (e.g., visual proofs not judged as particularly explanatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or researching explanatoriness, rely on empirical judgments and be cautious about assumed explanatory status of proof types; examine what features mathematicians actually use to judge explanation (e.g., logical structure).
